## NGO Website Development in India: Why Google Ad Grants Puts Your Website on the Line

Google Ad Grants gives eligible non-profits up to $10,000 a month in free Google Search advertising, but the program is enforced through website-quality rules, not just campaign settings. This means NGO website development in India has quietly become a compliance requirement for any organisation that wants to apply for the grant, keep it, or recover it after a suspension.

Most guidance on Ad Grants is written for the marketing team running the campaigns: keyword lists, ad copy, bidding strategy. That is only half the picture. Google's own account management and website policies place specific, checkable requirements on the site the ads point to — navigation, page content, HTTPS, conversion tracking, load speed, and the absence of ad-like design elements. An NGO can have a well-run Ads account and still lose its grant because the website behind it does not meet policy. This article walks through what those website-side requirements actually are, sourced from Google's own published policies, and what it means in practice for an Indian non-profit's site.

## What Google Ad Grants Offers Indian Non-Profits

Google Ad Grants provides qualifying non-profits with up to $10,000 per month in in-kind Google Search advertising, shown alongside regular paid results on Google.com. It is not a cash grant — it is ad inventory, spent through a standard Google Ads account that has grant-specific rules layered on top of it.

### Who qualifies in India

To be eligible for Google for Nonprofits (the prerequisite for Ad Grants) in India, an organisation generally needs to be registered as one of the following:

- A registered Society
- A registered Trust
- A Section 8 Company (previously Section 25 under the old Companies Act)

Google's India eligibility guidelines also require valid registration under the Foreign Contribution Regulation Act (FCRA) for organisations in this category. Government entities, hospitals and healthcare organisations, and schools, colleges or universities are generally excluded from the program, though charitable foundations affiliated with a hospital or the philanthropic arm of an educational institution may still qualify in some cases. NGOs working through FCRA registration should also be aware that FCRA compliance itself has been through recent regulatory changes — our separate piece on [FCRA amendment rules for NGO websites in India](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-fcra-amendment-rules-2026) covers what those changes mean for your site and disclosures.

### The verification step

Before an Ad Grants account can be created, the organisation must be verified as a legitimate non-profit through Google's designated validation partner. This verification step has changed hands over the years — Google's current published guidance for India routes this through its nonprofit verification partner, and organisations should expect to submit registration documents (society/trust/Section 8 certificate, FCRA registration where applicable, and PAN details) as part of that process. Because this partner and process can change, always confirm the current steps on Google's own Google for Nonprofits help pages rather than relying on older blog posts, which may describe an outdated verification workflow.

Once verified, the organisation applies for Google for Nonprofits, then separately enrols in the Ad Grants product inside that account and accepts the program's terms of service.

## The Account-Quality Rules Behind Every Ad Grants Suspension

Google reviews Ad Grants accounts on an ongoing basis, and a meaningful share of the rules it checks are directly about how the account is structured and how it performs — not just what the website looks like. Understanding these rules matters for website teams because several of them cannot be satisfied without changes to the site itself.

### Minimum click-through rate

Ad Grants accounts (other than those running exclusively on Smart campaigns) must maintain a 5% click-through rate at the account level each month. This is not a per-keyword requirement, but if the account average falls below 5% for two consecutive months, Google temporarily deactivates the grant. A low CTR is often a symptom of a website mismatch: ads promising something the destination page does not clearly deliver, or a homepage that does not match the search intent the ad was written for.

### Conversion tracking

For accounts created on or after 22 April 2019, Google requires at least one qualifying conversion action to be set up and to record a minimum of one conversion per month. Google's own guidance lists acceptable conversion types, including donations, purchases, ticket sales, membership sign-ups, volunteer sign-ups, petition signatures, newsletter sign-ups, and meaningful on-site engagement. Accounts created after that date are also required to use conversion-based Smart Bidding (such as Maximize Conversions or Target CPA), unless they run exclusively on Smart campaigns. Both requirements depend on the website having the right tracking code and a functioning action for someone to complete — this is fundamentally a website and analytics task, not something the marketing team can set up in the Ads interface alone.

### Keyword quality rules

Google's Ad Grants keyword policy restricts single-word keywords that are too broad to reflect a specific mission or intent, along with generic terms unrelated to charitable search intent (its published examples include phrases like "free videos" or "today's news"). A short, explicit list of exceptions exists for words like charity, donate, ngo, nonprofit and volunteer, along with an organisation's own brand terms and certain medical-condition terms. This rule affects site content indirectly: pages that are too thin or too generic to support a specific, mission-relevant keyword make it harder to build a compliant keyword list in the first place.

### Geographic targeting

Accounts are required to use proper location targeting, aimed at the places where the organisation's beneficiaries, donors or program areas actually are — not broad, worldwide targeting by default. For an Indian NGO working across a handful of states, or one raising funds domestically while running a program regionally, this needs to be reflected consistently across the Ads account and the website's own content (state or city names on relevant program pages, for example).

### Sitelink assets and account structure

Google's account management policy also requires accounts to maintain a minimum number of sitelink ad assets, meaning the website needs at least a couple of clearly distinct, relevant internal pages to link to beyond the homepage — donation page, volunteer page, program page, contact page, and similar.

## Ad Grants Website Requirements Checklist

The table below summarises the website-facing requirements that recur across Google's account management and website policies, translated into what they mean for the build itself.

| Ad Grants requirement | What it means for your site | How to check or fix it |
|---|---|---|
| Full-site HTTPS | Every page, not just the donation form, must load over a secure connection | Check the browser padlock on every template (home, program pages, blog, donation flow); redirect all HTTP requests to HTTPS at the server level |
| Substantial, original content | Thin pages, stock-text "About Us" copy, or pages that are mostly embedded video/links will not pass review | Rewrite mission, program, and about pages with specific, original detail about what the organisation actually does and where |
| Clear navigation and no broken links | Menus should be logical; every link, especially the donate button, must resolve correctly | Run a link checker quarterly; test the donation and contact flows manually, not just visually |
| Mobile-friendliness | Pages must display and function correctly on phones and tablets | Test on an actual phone, not just browser dev tools; check that forms and buttons are usable at small widths |
| Working donation or contact mechanism | There must be a functioning way for a visitor to take the action your ads promise | Submit a real test donation or enquiry end-to-end and confirm it is received and confirmed |
| Conversion tracking installed | Google Tag / Google Analytics must fire on the actual completed action, not just the page load | Verify conversions in Google Ads reporting, not only in Analytics, and confirm at least one fires per month |
| No ad-like design elements | Content designed to look like a native or paid ad unit (e.g. AdSense blocks) is disallowed on Ad Grants-funded traffic | Remove third-party ad networks from any page your grant campaigns can reach |
| Fast page load | Slow pages hurt both Quality Score and grant compliance review | Test with a free page-speed tool on the exact pages your ads point to, not just the homepage |
| Relevant geo-targeting reflected on-site | Ads should point to pages that make sense for the targeted location | Make sure program or chapter pages actually name the regions being targeted in the Ads account |

## Content, Navigation and Design: What Your Site Needs to Pass Review

### Depth over decoration

Google's website policy is explicit that a site needs "a significant amount of original content that is directly related to your nonprofit's mission." A single-page site, a template with placeholder text still in it, or a design-heavy homepage with almost no readable copy will not satisfy this. In practice this means writing real, specific pages: what the programs are, who they serve, where they operate, and what a rupee donated actually funds. Annual reports, registration numbers, and named leadership also strengthen a site's credibility during review.

### Navigation that supports the whole funnel

A visitor who clicks a search ad should be able to reach the donation page, a program page, and a contact page within one or two clicks from wherever they land. Broken navigation, dead links, or a donate button that leads to an error page are named directly in Google's guidance as compliance risks — and they are also, separately, the kind of thing that quietly kills conversion rate regardless of any grant.

### No ad-like elements

Sites that carry third-party ad networks (Google AdSense being the most commonly flagged) on pages reached through Ad Grants traffic are not compliant. This rule exists to keep grant-funded clicks landing on genuinely mission-focused content rather than monetised traffic, and it is worth checking for on any older NGO site that was previously supported through display advertising revenue.

### HTTPS and mobile as baseline, not bonus

HTTPS across the entire site, and correct rendering and function on phones and tablets, are treated as baseline requirements rather than best practices. For Indian NGOs, where a large share of search traffic — including traffic from Ad Grants campaigns — arrives on mobile devices, a site that is technically HTTPS-compliant but slow or awkward on a phone will still under-perform on the CTR and conversion metrics Google is actively measuring.

## Conversion Tracking Is a Development Task, Not a Marketing Checkbox

### Setting up Google Tag and GA4 correctly

Conversion tracking is frequently treated as a marketing-team configuration step, but it depends entirely on how the website is built. The Google Tag (or Google Analytics 4 event tracking, connected through to Google Ads) needs to fire specifically on completed actions: a successful donation, a submitted volunteer form, a confirmed newsletter sign-up. If the tag fires on page load instead of on actual completion, the account can show conversions that don't reflect real actions, which risks both non-compliance and wasted grant spend on things that aren't working.

This is squarely a development responsibility: the donation gateway's success page, the form's submit handler, and the site's tag manager configuration all need to be built (or audited, on an older site) with this specific event in mind, not bolted on afterward.

### Donation and enquiry mechanisms that actually work

A conversion goal is meaningless if the underlying action does not reliably work. Payment gateway failures, forms that silently fail to send, or donation pages that time out under load are common on NGO sites that were built quickly or have not been maintained. Before applying for or renewing an Ad Grant, it is worth testing the entire donation and contact path as an actual user would, including on mobile and on a slow connection, rather than assuming it works because it did at launch.

Organisations managing donor relationships alongside their website should also look at how donation and enquiry data flows into their CRM — our guide to [donor CRM software for NGOs in India](/blog/ngo-donor-crm-software-india-2026) goes into how that connects back to the same conversion data Ad Grants depends on.

## Why NGO Website Development in India Needs an Ad-Grants Lens From Day One

Treating Ad Grants compliance as something to retrofit after a website is built usually means redoing work: adding HTTPS to a site that launched without it, rewriting thin content pages, rebuilding a donation flow to support proper event tracking, or restructuring navigation to expose the pages Google's sitelink requirement expects. Each of these is more expensive after launch than during it.

This is why NGO website development in India increasingly needs to account for Ad Grants requirements at the planning stage, not just at the marketing stage — deciding the site's information architecture, its analytics setup, its hosting and SSL configuration, and its content plan with the program's rules already in mind. A broader look at how to plan an NGO site from scratch, independent of Ad Grants specifically, is covered in our [NGO website development guide for India](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-guide-2026).

It also means the people building and maintaining the site need at least a working understanding of the program's rules, since a change made for design reasons — removing a page, changing a form, switching hosts — can unintentionally break something Google is actively monitoring.

## How Govindani Infotech Approaches Ad-Grant-Ready Websites for Non-Profits

Having built websites for 160+ non-profits, our approach at Govindani Infotech treats Ad Grants readiness as a website-development decision, not an afterthought bolted on by a marketing agency once the grant is already at risk. When we scope a non-profit's site, we build in HTTPS and mobile responsiveness as defaults, structure navigation around the pages Google expects to see (mission, programs, donate, contact), and set up conversion tracking on the actual completed action — a successful donation or a submitted form — rather than a page view that only looks like engagement. We also write content plans with our clients so that program and mission pages carry real, specific detail instead of placeholder text, because that same substance is what both Google's reviewers and actual donors are looking for. Where a non-profit already has a Google Ad Grants account that is underperforming or at risk of suspension, we look at the website side of the account first, since that is where a large share of preventable suspensions originate. You can see more about how we approach non-profit sites on our [NGO website page](/pages/ngopage/).

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Does my NGO need 80G, 12A or FCRA registration to get Google Ad Grants in India?

Google's India eligibility guidelines require registration as a Society, Trust, or Section 8 Company, along with valid FCRA registration for organisations that fall under it. Tax registrations like 80G and 12A are commonly requested as supporting documentation during the broader non-profit verification process, though the exact document list can change, so it is worth checking Google's current published guidance before applying.

### Is the Google Ad Grant really free, and is there a catch?

The grant itself is genuinely in-kind advertising spend — up to $10,000 a month in Google Search ads — at no cost to the non-profit. The "catch," if there is one, is that the account is held to specific ongoing compliance rules (minimum click-through rate, conversion tracking, keyword restrictions, and website quality standards), and accounts that don't meet them get temporarily deactivated or suspended.

### Can Ad Grants campaigns run ads specifically for fundraising or donation campaigns?

Yes, donations are one of the conversion types Google explicitly recognises, and driving traffic to a donation page is a common and accepted use of Ad Grants. What matters is that the donation page itself is functional, secure, and set up with proper conversion tracking so the completed donation is recorded as the goal, not just the click.

### What causes most Ad Grant account suspensions that trace back to the website?

Based on the account and website policies Google publishes, the most common website-related causes are thin or generic content, broken links (particularly on donation or contact pages), missing HTTPS, and conversion tracking that either isn't installed or isn't firing on a real completed action. A mismatch between what the ad promises and what the landing page actually delivers also tends to depress click-through rate below the required threshold.

### Do we need a fully built website before applying for Ad Grants, or can we build it afterward?

A functional, content-substantial, HTTPS-secured website is generally expected as part of qualifying for and maintaining the grant, since Google reviews the site the ads point to as part of ongoing compliance. It is more practical, and usually less costly, to have the website in a compliant state before applying rather than scrambling to fix navigation, content, or tracking gaps after an account is flagged.

### How is Google Ad Grants different from running regular paid Google Ads for an NGO?

Ad Grants is a separate, in-kind program with its own account structure, its own stricter policy set (the 5% CTR rule, keyword restrictions, and conversion tracking mandate among them), and a spending cap. A non-profit is free to run a normal paid Google Ads account alongside or instead of Ad Grants, and the two can be used for different goals, but they are governed by different rule sets and should generally be managed with that distinction clearly understood.

## Where to Start

If your organisation is applying for Google Ad Grants for the first time, start by auditing your current site against the checklist above — HTTPS across every page, a working donation or contact flow, real content on your mission and program pages, and conversion tracking that fires on the completed action rather than the page view. If you already hold a grant and have received a compliance warning or suspension notice, the fastest path back to good standing is usually a website-side review before touching the Ads account itself, since that is where most preventable issues originate.
